title: At the station
goal: Buy tickets, ask about times and platforms, and use ordinal numbers.
bekal: buying a train or bus ticket
asking departure times and journey length

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En la estación
dialogs.intro: Buying a ticket. A conversation that goes almost the same way everywhere.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Buenos días. Un billete para Sevilla, por favor.
lines.id: Good morning. A ticket to Seville, please.
lines.literal: good day. a ticket for Seville, please.

lines.speaker: Taquillera:
lines.text: ¿De ida o de ida y vuelta?
lines.literal: of going or of going and return?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: De ida y vuelta. Vuelvo el domingo.
lines.id: Round trip. I'm coming back on Sunday.
lines.literal: of going and return. I-return the Sunday.

lines.speaker: Taquillera:
lines.text: ¿Para qué hora? Hay uno a las nueve y otro a las once.
lines.id: For what time? There's one at nine and another at eleven.
lines.literal: for what time? there-is one at the nine and other at the eleven.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: The nine o'clock. How long does it take?
lines.literal: the of the nine. how-much it-takes?

lines.speaker: Taquillera:
lines.text: Dos horas y media. Llega a las once y media.
lines.id: Two and a half hours. It arrives at half past eleven.
lines.literal: two hours and half. it-arrives at the eleven and half.

lines.speaker: Taquillera:
lines.text: Sesenta y cuatro euros. ¿Ventanilla o pasillo?
lines.literal: sixty and four euros. little-window or aisle?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ventanilla, por favor. ¿De qué andén sale?
lines.id: Window, please. Which platform does it leave from?
lines.literal: little-window, please. from what platform it-leaves?

lines.speaker: Taquillera:
lines.text: Del andén cuatro. Suba diez minutos antes.
lines.id: Platform four. Board ten minutes before.
lines.literal: from-the platform four. get-on(formal) ten minutes before.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Gracias. Una última cosa: ¿hay wifi en el tren?
lines.id: Thank you. One last thing: is there wifi on the train?
lines.literal: thanks. one last thing: there-is wifi on the train?

lines.speaker: Taquillera:
lines.id: Yes, it's free. Have a good trip.

notes: **Un billete para Sevilla.** A ticket's destination takes *para*, not *a*: *un billete para Madrid*, *un billete para las nueve*. The movement itself takes *a*: *voy a Sevilla*.
**De ida / de ida y vuelta** = one-way / round trip. In Latin America a ticket is *el boleto* or *el pasaje*, not *el billete*.

**El de las nueve** = "the nine o'clock one". The pattern *el de…* and *la de…* replaces a noun that's already clear: *la de azul* (the one in blue), *el de Marta* (Marta's). Very common and a great word-saver.
**Otro without an article.** *Hay otro a las once*, not *un otro*. Almost every beginner makes this mistake, tempted by English "another".
**Tardar vs durar.** *¿Cuánto tarda?* asks how long the trip takes you; *¿cuánto dura?* asks how long something lasts — a film, a class, a show.
**Suba** is the polite command of *subir*. What staff say at stations and airports is almost all polite commands, so recognizing the form matters more than producing it.
**Antes / después** stand alone as adverbs (*diez minutos antes*), and take *de* before a noun or verb: *antes de salir*, *después de la plaza*.
**Buen viaje** — *bueno* shortens to *buen* before a masculine singular noun, as in *un buen día*, *un buen restaurante*. The feminine stays whole: *una buena idea*.

grammars.title: Ordinal numbers
body: After tenth, even native speakers rarely use ordinals — they go back to plain numbers: *el piso once*, *la calle veinte*.
after: Only *primero* and *tercero* shorten, and only before a masculine singular noun. Standing alone, they stay whole: *¿Cuál tomo? —El primero.*
For building floors, remember the warning from Unit 12: *la planta baja* is the ground floor, so *el primer piso* is what Americans call the second floor.

blocks.text: Notice *salida* appears twice with different meanings — departure on a timetable board, exit in a building. Context tells them apart, and both come from the same verb: *salir*.

blocks.title: Asking the way without a map
items: People in Spain and Latin America almost always stop and answer when asked the way — often walking a few steps with you. Opening with *perdone* or *disculpe* is all it takes.
One risk: many people would rather guess than admit they don't know. If the directions sound unsure, ask a second person.
Distances are rarely given in meters; almost always in minutes on foot. *Está a diez minutos* can mean anything from seven to twenty minutes.
In big Spanish cities, bus and metro tickets can usually be paid with a bank card right at the entrance. In small towns, have cash ready — bus drivers don't always have change for big notes.

items: Hay uno a las nueve y otro a las once.
